intro: People all over the world care for their health. In China, people do tai chi in parks. In India, people stretch with yoga. Families everywhere share warm soup and rest.
You can help keep yourself safe too. You can wear a helmet. You can buckle up. You can learn stop, drop and roll. You can find a safe adult.
In this unit, you will learn healthy ways from around the world. You will learn how to stay safe each day. You will know who to ask for help.
bigQuestion: How do people around the world stay well and safe?

timeline.t: Wake up after a good night of sleep.
Stretch with a yoga tree pose or slow tai chi moves.
Buckle up in the back seat for the ride to school.
Hold a grown-up's hand and cross at the crosswalk.
Put on sunscreen and a hat before playing outside.
Put on a helmet before riding a bike or scooter.
Eat a warm dinner with family, maybe with spices.
Practice the fire escape plan and your address.

slow, gentle moves done with calm breathing
stretching and holding shapes while breathing slowly
something that helps you feel better
testing ideas to find out what is true
a hard hat that protects your head
a lotion that helps keep the sun from burning your skin
a grown-up you can trust to help you

test.why: Turmeric is a yellow spice from a root, used in India.

test.why: Indigenous peoples are the first peoples of a land.

test.q: What helps your body heal when you are sick?
Why tell your doctor about teas and herbs?
test.why: Doctors ask about home remedies to keep you safe.

test.q: What do you wear on your head when you ride a scooter?
test.why: A helmet protects your head if you fall.

test.q: Where do kids ride in a car?
test.why: Kids ride buckled up in the back seat.

choices: Do not touch and tell a grown-up

test.why: Stop, drop and roll puts out the flames.

Tell where you learned about it.

title: Healthy Ways Around the World

chapters.title: Old Ways of Staying Well
chapters.bigQuestion: How have people around the world helped each other stay well?

story.title: Slow Moves in the Park
story.kicker: Nai Nai shows Leo a calm way to start the day.
paragraphs: It is early morning in a Chicago park. The grass is wet. Leo holds his grandmother's hand. He calls her Nai Nai. That means grandma in Chinese.
A group of people stand under the trees. They move their arms very slowly. They step softly, like cats. Nai Nai says, "This is tai chi."
Leo tries it. He lifts his arms like a bird. He breathes in and out. He wobbles, then he stands tall. Nai Nai smiles at him.
"My grandma taught me this in China," Nai Nai says. "Now I teach you." Leo feels calm and warm. He wants to come back tomorrow.
story.think: What does your family do to feel calm or stay well?

lessons.title: People Everywhere Care
lessons.mainIdea: People all over the world have cared for their health for a very long time.
reading: Long, long ago, people got sick, just like today. They got scrapes and coughs. They wanted to feel better.
So people everywhere found ways to stay well. They rested. They ate good food. They helped each other. Caring for *health* is very old.
Families passed these ways down. Grandparents taught parents. Parents taught children. Now you are learning too.

words.d: how well your body and mind are doing

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Picture a family long ago. A child has a cough. The mother wraps the child in a warm blanket. The grandfather brings a cup of warm water. Everyone stays close.
look.prompt: How is this family helping the child feel better?

check.q: Who has cared for health for a long time?
check.why: The reading says people everywhere have cared for health for a very long time.

check.q: What does the word health mean?
choices: How well your body and mind are doing
check.why: Health means how well your body and mind are doing.

check.q: How did families share ways to stay well?
check.why: The reading says grandparents taught parents, and parents taught children.

lessons.title: Tea and Tai Chi
lessons.mainIdea: In China, many people drink tea and do tai chi, slow gentle moves.
reading: In China, many people drink tea. Tea is made from leaves and hot water. Families sip tea together.
Many people also do *tai chi* in parks. Tai chi is slow, gentle moving. People breathe calmly as they move.
Scientists have studied tai chi. It can help people keep their balance. Older people often like it.

words.d: slow, gentle moves done with calm breathing
staying steady so you do not fall

look.title: What Scientists Found
look.text: Tai chi may help older people keep their balance and fall less.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (U.S.), Tai Chi: What You Need To Know
look.prompt: Why might tai chi be good for a grandparent?

check.q: What is tai chi?
check.why: Tai chi is slow, gentle moving with calm breathing.

check.q: Where do many people in China do tai chi?
check.why: The reading says many people do tai chi in parks.

check.q: What can tai chi help people keep?
check.why: Scientists found tai chi can help people keep their balance.

lessons.title: Stretching with Yoga
lessons.mainIdea: In India, many people do yoga to stretch, breathe and feel calm.
reading: Yoga comes from India. It is very old. Today people all over the world do it, even kids.
In *yoga*, you hold your body in shapes. One shape looks like a tree. You stand on one foot. You breathe slowly.
Yoga helps you stretch. Slow breathing can help you feel calm. You can try it at home or at school.

words.d: stretching and holding shapes while breathing slowly
to reach your body out long

look.title: Tree Pose
look.text: Stand tall. Put one foot on your other leg, below the knee. Put your hands together. Look at one spot on the wall. Breathe in. Breathe out. Now switch feet.
look.prompt: How did your body feel when you tried tree pose?

check.q: Where does yoga come from?
check.why: The reading says yoga comes from India.

check.q: What do you do in yoga?
check.why: In yoga you hold your body in shapes and breathe slowly.

check.q: What can slow breathing help you feel?
check.why: The reading says slow breathing can help you feel calm.

lessons.title: Spices in Food
lessons.mainIdea: In India, many people cook with spices like turmeric.
reading: Smell a pot of Indian curry. It smells warm and good. It has many *spices* in it.
One spice is *turmeric*. It is bright yellow. It comes from a root. It makes rice and curry yellow.
Many families in India have used turmeric for a long time. Scientists are still learning what it does. Ask a doctor before using any spice as medicine.

words.d: a part of a plant used to give food flavor
a yellow spice that comes from a root

look.title: A Yellow Plate
look.text: Look at a plate of rice. The rice is bright yellow. A little turmeric was cooked with it. It smells warm. Next to it is a bowl of beans and a piece of flat bread.

check.q: What color is turmeric?
check.why: Turmeric is a bright yellow spice.

check.q: Where does turmeric come from?
check.why: The reading says turmeric comes from a root.

check.q: Who should you ask before using a spice as medicine?
check.why: The reading says to ask a doctor before using any spice as medicine.

lessons.title: Plants People Knew
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous peoples in the Americas knew many plants very well.
reading: *Indigenous peoples* are the first peoples of a land. In the Americas, they lived here long before others came.
They watched plants closely for many years. They knew which plants were food. They knew which plants could help, and which could hurt.
Some plants can make you sick. So never eat a wild plant. Only trusted adults who know plants should pick them.

words.d: the first peoples who lived on a land

look.title: A Walk in the Woods
look.text: A grandmother walks in the woods with a child. She points to a plant. She says its name. She tells how her people used it. The child looks, but does not touch or eat it.
look.prompt: Why does the child only look and not eat the plant?

check.q: Who are Indigenous peoples?
choices: The first peoples of a land
check.why: Indigenous peoples are the first peoples of a land.

check.q: How did Indigenous peoples learn about plants?
choices: By watching them closely for many years
check.why: The reading says they watched plants closely for many years.

check.q: What should you do with a wild plant?
check.why: Some plants can make you sick, so never eat a wild plant.

lessons.title: Soup and Rest
lessons.mainIdea: Grandparents often share remedies like warm soup and rest.
reading: You have a cold. Grandpa makes warm chicken soup. You drink it slowly. It feels good on your throat.
Soup and rest are *remedies*. A remedy is something that helps you feel better. Many families have their own.
Rest is very important. Sleep helps your body heal. Kids need lots of sleep each night.

words.d: something that helps you feel better
to get well again

look.title: How Much Sleep Kids Need
look.unit: hours of sleep a night, at least
look.cite: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, sleep recommendations for children, 2016
look.prompt: Find your age. How many hours of sleep do you need?

check.q: What is a remedy?
choices: Something that helps you feel better
check.why: A remedy is something that helps you feel better.

check.q: What helps your body heal?
check.why: The reading says sleep helps your body heal.

check.q: Kids ages 6 to 12 need at least how many hours of sleep?
check.why: The chart shows kids ages 6 to 12 need at least 9 hours.

lessons.title: Doctors Today
lessons.mainIdea: Doctors today learn from science and ask about home remedies.
reading: Maya visits the doctor. The doctor listens to her heart. Then the doctor asks, "What do you do at home when you feel sick?"
Doctors learn from *science*. Science means testing ideas to see what works. Doctors use what the tests show.
Doctors also want to know about teas, herbs and home remedies. Tell your doctor what you use. That helps them keep you safe.

words.d: testing ideas to find out what is true
a person trained to help sick people get well

look.title: At the Doctor
look.text: Maya's dad tells the doctor, "We give her honey tea for coughs." The doctor nods and writes it down. "Thank you for telling me," the doctor says.
look.prompt: Why is it good that Maya's dad told the doctor about the tea?

check.q: What do doctors learn from?
check.why: The reading says doctors learn from science.

check.q: What does science mean?
choices: Testing ideas to see what works
check.why: Science means testing ideas to see what works.

check.q: Why tell your doctor about home remedies?
choices: It helps them keep you safe
check.why: The reading says telling your doctor helps them keep you safe.

review.why: Tai chi is slow, gentle moving from China.
Turmeric is a bright yellow spice from a root.

review.q: What should you never do with a wild plant?
review.why: Some plants can make you sick, so never eat a wild plant.

review.q: Which is a remedy many grandparents share?
review.why: Soup and rest are remedies that help you feel better.

review.q: What should you tell your doctor about?
review.why: Doctors want to know about home remedies to keep you safe.

chapters.title: Staying Safe
chapters.bigQuestion: What can I do to keep myself safe every day?

story.title: Rosa Leads the Way
story.kicker: A family practices getting out of the house, and the youngest shows the way.
paragraphs: Beep, beep, beep! Mom pushes the smoke alarm button. "This is only practice," she says. "Let's try our fire escape plan."
Rosa is the youngest. She is six. She knows the plan. "Get low and go!" she calls. She crawls to the front door. Her big brother follows.
Rosa does not stop for her toys. She goes straight outside. She walks to the big tree by the sidewalk. That is the meeting spot.
Everyone is at the tree. Dad counts: one, two, three, four. "Rosa, you led the way!" he says. Rosa grins. She knows just what to do.
story.think: Where is your family's meeting spot outside your home?

lessons.title: Helmets On
lessons.mainIdea: Wear a helmet every time you ride a bike or scooter.
reading: Jamal gets his bike. Before he rides, he puts on his *helmet*. He clicks the strap under his chin.
A helmet is a hard hat. It protects your head if you fall. Your brain is inside your head, so it needs care.
Wear a helmet on bikes, scooters and skates. It should sit flat and snug. A grown-up can help it fit.

words.d: a hard hat that protects your head
to keep safe from harm

look.title: Ready to Ride
look.text: Look at two kids with scooters. Ana has a helmet on. The strap is clicked under her chin. Ben's helmet is in his hand. He is about to ride.
look.prompt: What should Ben do before he rides?

check.q: What does a helmet protect?
check.why: A helmet protects your head if you fall.

check.q: When should you wear a helmet?
choices: Every time you ride a bike or scooter
check.why: The reading says to wear a helmet on bikes, scooters and skates.

check.q: Where does the helmet strap click?
check.why: Jamal clicks the strap under his chin.

lessons.title: Buckle Up
lessons.mainIdea: Car seats and seat belts keep you safe in a car.
reading: Click! Before the car moves, everyone buckles up. Little kids ride in a *car seat*. Bigger kids use a booster seat.
A *seat belt* holds you in place. If the car stops fast, it keeps you in your seat.
Kids ride in the back seat. Buckle up on every trip, even short ones. The driver buckles up too.

words.d: a special seat that keeps young kids safe in a car
a strap that holds you in your seat

look.title: A Safety Rule
look.text: Children under 13 should ride buckled up in the back seat.
look.cite: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (U.S.), Car Seats and Booster Seats
look.prompt: Where should kids your age sit in a car?

check.q: What does a seat belt do?
check.why: A seat belt holds you in place if the car stops fast.

check.q: Where do kids ride in a car?
check.why: The reading says kids ride in the back seat.

check.q: When should you buckle up?
check.why: The reading says buckle up on every trip, even short ones.

lessons.title: Crossing the Street
lessons.mainIdea: Hold a grown-up's hand, stop, and look both ways before you cross.
reading: Mia and her dad reach the corner. They stop at the curb. Mia holds Dad's hand tight.
They look left. They look right. They look left again. They listen for cars. They cross at the *crosswalk*.
Watch the walk signal. A walking person means go. A hand means stop and wait on the curb.

words.d: the marked place on a street where people cross
the edge of the sidewalk next to the street

look.title: At the Corner
look.text: Picture a busy corner. White stripes go across the street. A light shows a red hand. A bus rolls by. A girl and her grandpa wait on the curb.
look.prompt: What should the girl and her grandpa do right now?

check.q: Where should you cross the street?
choices: In the middle of the block
check.why: Mia and her dad cross at the crosswalk.

check.q: What should you do before you cross?
choices: Look left, right and left again
check.why: The reading says to look left, right, and left again.

check.q: What does a hand on the walk signal mean?
check.why: A hand means stop and wait on the curb.

lessons.title: Sunscreen and Hats
lessons.mainIdea: Sunscreen, hats and shade protect your skin from the sun.
reading: It is a hot day at the beach. Grandma rubs *sunscreen* on Leo's arms. She puts on his sun hat.
The sun can burn your skin. A sunburn is red and sore. Sunscreen is a lotion that helps stop sunburn.
Put sunscreen on before you go out. Put more on after you swim. Rest in the shade too.

words.d: a lotion that helps keep the sun from burning your skin
a cool spot out of the sun

look.title: Sunscreen Tips
look.cite: American Academy of Dermatology, How to Apply Sunscreen
look.prompt: How often should you put on more sunscreen?

check.q: What does sunscreen help stop?
check.why: Sunscreen is a lotion that helps stop sunburn.

check.q: When should you put on more sunscreen?
check.why: The reading says to put more on after you swim.

check.q: What is shade?
choices: A cool spot out of the sun
check.why: Shade is a cool spot out of the sun.

lessons.title: Grown-Ups Only
lessons.mainIdea: Only grown-ups handle medicine and cleaning products.
reading: Sam sees a bottle under the sink. It has bright colors. It looks like juice. Sam does not touch it. He tells Mom.
*Cleaning products* can hurt your body. Medicine can hurt you too if you take the wrong kind or too much.
Only trusted grown-ups give *medicine*. If you find a bottle or pills, do not touch. Tell a grown-up.

words.d: something a doctor or grown-up gives to help you get well
soaps and sprays used to clean, not to eat or drink

look.title: What Would You Do?
look.text: You are playing at a friend's house. You find a little bottle of pills on the floor. They are pink, like candy. Your friend says, "Let's try one!"
look.prompt: What should you say and do?

check.q: Who should give you medicine?
check.why: The reading says only trusted grown-ups give medicine.

check.q: What should you do if you find pills?
choices: Do not touch and tell a grown-up
check.why: The reading says do not touch, and tell a grown-up.

check.q: What did Sam do when he saw the bottle?
check.why: Sam did not touch the bottle. He told Mom.

lessons.title: Fire Safety
lessons.mainIdea: If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.
reading: A *smoke alarm* beeps loudly when there is smoke. When you hear it, get out fast. Go to your meeting spot.
If your clothes catch fire, do not run. *Stop, drop and roll.* Stop where you are. Drop to the ground. Cover your face and roll.
Rolling puts out the flames. Practice it with your family. Then you will know what to do.

words.d: a machine that beeps loudly when it senses smoke
what to do if your clothes catch fire

look.title: Fire Safety Steps
look.text: If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop to the ground, cover your face with your hands, and roll over and over until the fire is out.
look.cite: National Fire Protection Association, Stop, Drop and Roll safety tip sheet
look.prompt: Why do you cover your face when you roll?

check.q: What should you do if your clothes catch fire?
check.why: The reading says stop, drop and roll.

check.q: What does a smoke alarm do?
choices: Beeps loudly when there is smoke
check.why: A smoke alarm beeps loudly when there is smoke.

check.q: What puts out the flames on your clothes?
check.why: The reading says rolling puts out the flames.

lessons.title: Know Your Address
lessons.mainIdea: Learn your address and a grown-up's phone number.
reading: Your *address* tells where your home is. It has a house number, a street and a town.
If you get lost, your address helps a safe grown-up take you home. A phone number helps them call your family.
Practice saying your address. Sing it like a song. In an emergency, a grown-up can call 911.

words.d: the number, street and town where your home is
a time when someone needs help right away

look.title: Parts of an Address
look.text: Look at a letter. On it are the words: 25 Maple Street, Springfield. The number is 25. The street is Maple Street. The town is Springfield.
look.prompt: Can you say the three parts of your own address?

check.q: What does your address tell?
check.why: Your address tells where your home is.

check.q: What are the parts of an address?
choices: A number, a street and a town
check.why: An address has a number, a street and a town.

check.q: What number can a grown-up call in an emergency?
check.why: The reading says a grown-up can call 911 in an emergency.

lessons.title: Safe Grown-Ups
lessons.mainIdea: Safe adults help you, and you can always tell them when something feels wrong.
reading: Kai gets lost at the store. He looks around. He sees a worker with a name tag. He asks her for help.
A *safe adult* is a grown-up you can trust. Parents, teachers, school nurses and police officers can be safe adults.
If something feels wrong, tell a safe adult. If a secret makes you feel bad, tell. Safe adults will listen.

words.d: a grown-up you can trust to help you
to believe someone will do right by you

look.title: My Safe Adults
look.text: Draw a hand. On each finger, write or draw one safe adult. Maybe Mom, Grandpa, your teacher, the school nurse or a neighbor. Now you have five people to go to.
look.prompt: Who are the five safe adults on your hand?

check.q: What is a safe adult?
check.why: A safe adult is a grown-up you can trust.

check.q: Who did Kai ask for help?
choices: A worker with a name tag
check.why: Kai asked a store worker with a name tag.

check.q: What should you do if a secret makes you feel bad?
check.why: The reading says if a secret makes you feel bad, tell a safe adult.

review.why: A helmet protects your head on bikes and scooters.

review.q: What holds you in your seat in a car?
review.why: A seat belt holds you in place.

review.q: What do you do if your clothes catch fire?
review.why: Stop, drop and roll puts out the flames.
Cleaning products can hurt you, so only grown-ups handle them.

review.q: What helps protect your skin at the beach?
review.why: Sunscreen, hats and shade protect your skin from the sun.

review.q: In the story, where did Rosa go after she got outside?
choices: To the meeting spot by the tree
review.why: Rosa walked to the big tree, the family's meeting spot.
